prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which opened the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: Twisted bilayer graphene is the kind of result I trust most: a simple mechanism, interlayer moire hybridisation that quenches the Dirac velocity at a magic angle, was derived analytically from a continuum model and then confirmed by the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018. The theory is understood rather than merely observed, and it has been reproduced by many groups and in several platforms in under a decade. It created a tunable, strongly correlated materials platform that links condensed-matter theory to statistical-physics questions about interaction-driven order. Having reread colleagues' attribution arguments, I now think the theory side should credit both authors of the continuum-model paper: the Bistritzer-MacDonald result is a single joint calculation, and leaving Bistritzer out would be hard to defend on the question of who first identified the mechanism. The experimental side rests with Jarillo-Herrero's group.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and attribution of the experiment. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so the compound discovery is not yet fully understood, which is the standard I apply to other candidates. The first experimental author of the key 2018 papers is not among the credited names and a three-person cap cannot represent junior contributors. Optical lattice clocks (B031) are, by contrast, mature, reproduced at the 1e-18 level in many laboratories, and have an uncontested two-person attribution. If the committee weights maturity and attribution cleanliness above conceptual novelty, B031 is the safer choice, and I do not want to dismiss that.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B031 first on clean attribution and broad independent reproduction, and places B024 sixth as scientifically strong but young, with the pairing mechanism and phase diagram unsettled.
responses.response: I accept the maturity point and the unsettled pairing mechanism is a real caveat. But the prize-worthy discovery is the flat band and the correlated states it hosts, not the pairing mechanism, and that core picture is stable and has been reproduced by many groups for years. I also disagree mildly that a clock is the more original result: the magic-wavelength idea is elegant, but it refines a measurement line honoured in 2005 and 2012, whereas moire flat bands opened a new class of correlated matter. I rank B031 lower than you do mainly for that novelty reason, and I take your argument seriously enough to name it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B024 first as a clean case of a continuum-band-theory prediction meeting a striking experiment, with theory plus experiment fitting a three-person prize including Bistritzer.
responses.response: I largely agree, and your attribution argument moves me on Bistritzer: the magic-angle result is a joint two-author calculation, so I now include him in the preferred configuration. I disagree only with your more optimistic reading of timing: the unresolved superconducting pairing means we should phrase the citation around the flat bands and the correlated states, not around a mechanism for superconductivity.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery (B005) first as the natural experimental completion of the 2013 prize, mature and confirmed by two independent detectors, with three of four credited leaders forming the trio.
responses.response: I agree that the science is beyond question and fully mature, and I ranked B005 fourth for that reason. My reservation is attribution: a three-person split between ATLAS and CMS leadership is arbitrary, and I cannot assess it as an outsider to particle physics. You note that Tejinder Virdee and Gianotti are both defensible, which tells me the committee cannot make that allocation on scientific grounds alone. I would not make B005 my preferred configuration unless colleagues can show a principled credit rule.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B031 first and B028 second, valuing the exquisite theory-experiment agreement in clocks and the control of every parameter in optical-lattice Hubbard simulators.
responses.response: I agree that B028 is a good bridge between statistical-physics models and experiment, which is why I ranked it third. My concern is the five credited names and the missing proposer Jaksch; you correctly note that the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Zoller and Cirac is painful. I opened with Esslinger in place of Zoller for experimental decisiveness, but I admit the theory-versus-experiment balance is not settled, and I do not think it beats B024 on conceptual novelty relative to the 2001 and 1997 prizes.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B009) first as a clear instrument advance that changed what can be seen, with a clean three-person Rose, Urban, Haider split.
responses.response: I recognise the technical achievement and the clean attribution. My own view is that I would give priority to a discovery of new physics over an enabling instrument, and B009 sits close to the boundary between technique and physics discovery, which you flag yourself. I did not rank it, but I take it as a serious candidate if the committee prefers a mature, uncontested prize.

uncertainties: Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene makes the discovery premature for 2026.
Whether credit for the 2018 experiments can be fairly allocated when the first experimental author is outside the credited names.
Whether Bistritzer should be included alongside MacDonald, which I now judge yes, versus a two-person theory-experiment pairing.
How the committee should weigh B031's strong support and clean attribution against B024's greater conceptual novelty.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I note that Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson are colleagues in the Gothenburg physics environment, but I have no specific collaboration with them or with any credited candidate that would require recusal.
